query: What does it mean for a startup to be 'ramen profitable'?
expected_answer: Ramen profitable means the startup makes just enough money to cover the founders' living expenses -- not full traditional profitability. Its main value isn't the money itself but that it buys the company time and reduces the pressure to raise more funding on someone else's schedule.

source: https://paulgraham.com/ramenprofitable.html

July 2009  
Now that the term "ramen profitable" has become widespread, I ought
to explain precisely what the idea entails.  
Ramen profitable means a startup makes just enough to pay the
founders' living expenses. This is a different form of profitability
than startups have traditionally aimed for. Traditional profitability
means a big bet is finally paying off, whereas the main importance
of ramen profitability is that it buys you time.
[[1](#f1n)]  
In the past, a startup would usually become profitable only
after raising and spending quite a lot of money. A company making
computer hardware might not become profitable for 5 years, during
which they spent $50 million. But when they did
they might have revenues of $50 million a year. This kind of
profitability means the startup has succeeded.  
Ramen profitability is the other extreme: a startup that becomes
profitable after 2 months, even though its revenues are only $3000
a month, because the only employees are a couple 25 year old founders
who can live on practically nothing. Revenues of $3000 a month do
not mean the company has succeeded.

Ramen profitability is an unfamiliar idea to most people because
it only recently became feasible. It's still not feasible for a
lot of startups; it would not be for most biotech startups, for
example; but it is for many software startups because they're now
so cheap. For many, the only real cost is the founders'

The main significance of this type of profitability is that you're

You can still raise money, but you don't have to do it now.

you can get better terms. If investors know you need money, they'll
sometimes take advantage of you. Some may even deliberately
stall, because they know that as you run out of money you'll become
increasingly pliable.

response:
Based on the essay by Paul Graham, **"ramen profitable"** means a startup makes just enough revenue to pay for the founders' living expenses.

Here are the key characteristics:

**What It Means:**
- Revenue is minimal but covers basic survival costs (hence the name, referencing instant ramen—the cheapest food available)
- Example: A startup with only two 25-year-old founders earning $3,000/month in revenue could be ramen profitable if that covers their expenses
- Revenues at this level don't indicate the company has "succeeded" in a traditional sense

**The Core Advantage:**
The main value isn't the absolute revenue—it's **buying time and independence**. Once a startup is ramen profitable:
- Founders no longer need to raise money to survive
- They're not at the mercy of investors
- They have better negotiating positions if they do seek investment
- They avoid the painful choice of either raising money or shutting down

**Why It Matters:**
This became possible recently due to low-cost software startups. In the past, startups typically required massive capital investment before becoming profitable. Now, many software startups need only the founders' living expenses to sustain themselves.

**The Warning:**
The main danger is sliding into consulting work instead of building a scalable product. While consulting can easily generate $3,000/month, it doesn't scale like a product business does. Ramen profitability is meant to be a stepping stone on the path to real growth—not the final destination.
